Q1. Which of the following statements about simplifying assumptions in mechanics is most reasonable?
A. We can model a hummingbird’s wing as a point mass when predicting the detailed bending motion during a wingbeat.
This confuses whole-body motion modeling with the need for an extended-body model to capture wing deformation.
B. We can model a city bus as a point mass when tracking its position change over several kilometers on a map.
Over kilometer-scale travel the bus’s size is negligible compared with the distance, so a point-mass model is appropriate.
C. We are never allowed to treat the surroundings as a vacuum, even if we intend to neglect air drag in a calculation.
This is incorrect because “vacuum” is often used as an idealization to ignore air resistance when it is negligible.
D. None of the above statements is correct.
Option B is a valid modeling approximation, so “none” is not correct.

Q2. Which of the following equations is correct?
A. 1 mm = 1 m
This ignores the metric prefix and incorrectly treats a millimeter as a meter.
B. 1 = 0.001
This incorrectly equates two pure numbers with different values without units.
C. 1 mm = 0.001 m
Since 1 m = 1000 mm, one millimeter equals 10−3 meters.
D. 1000 mm = 0.001 m
This inverts the conversion factor because 1000 mm = 1 m, not 0.001 m.

Q3. Which option has the incorrect unit?
A. Power: watt
A watt is correctly the SI unit of power (J/s).
B. Momentum: kilogram· meter/second
Momentum correctly has units of kg m/s.
C. Pressure: newton/meter
Pressure should be force per area (N/m2), so N/m is dimensionally wrong.
D. Electric potential: joule/coulomb
A volt is correctly J/C, so this unit matches electric potential.

Q7. A soccer ball is kicked with a launch speed v0 at an angle θ above the
horizontal (neglect air resistance). What is the speed of the ball at its maximum
height?
A. v0
This ignores that the vertical component of velocity decreases to zero at the top.
B. v0 cos θ
At maximum height the vertical velocity is zero, so the speed equals the unchanged horizontal
component v0 cos θ.
C. v0 sin θ
This confuses the initial vertical component with the speed at the peak, where the vertical
component is actually zero.
D. 0
Only the vertical component becomes zero at the top; the horizontal component remains
nonzero.

Q11. The force F⃗ = (2.50 N)ˆı + (6.00 N)ˆȷ acts on a particle as it moves along
the x axis from x = −1.2 m to x = 3.8 m. What is the work, in joules, done by
the force on the particle?
A. 12.5 J
Because the displacement is along x, W = F⃗ · ∆⃗r = Fx∆x = 2.50 × (3.8 − (−1.2)) = 12.5 J.
B. 30.0 J
This incorrectly uses only the y-component of force even though there is no y-displacement.
C. 42.5 J
This mistakenly adds components (or magnitudes) instead of taking the dot product with the
displacement direction.
D. 7.5 J
This comes from using an incorrect displacement (e.g., forgetting that ∆x spans from -1.2 m to
3.8 m).

Q12. A 3.0 kg cart initially moving at 4.0 m/s collides with a bumper and
rebounds at a speed of 1.5 m/s in the opposite direction. The collision lasts for
0.10 seconds. What is the average force exerted on the cart during the collision
(magnitude)?
A. 75 N
This corresponds to using only mvi/∆t and ignores the rebound (the final velocity).
B. 135 N
This results from using ∆v = 4.5 m/s (adding speeds but not accounting correctly for opposite
directions).
C. 165 N
Using impulse, |Favg| = m|∆v|/∆t = 3.0 |(−1.5 − 4.0)|/0.10 = 165 N.
D. None of the above is correct.
Option C matches the impulse/average-force calculation, so “none” is not correct.
